description: A fragment of the front cover. At the left is the bold heading "Centre Stamp"; beside it the lower two-thirds of an empty black-outlined rectangle (the stamp box), its top edge sliced off by the crop. The lower half of the crop is a pink curved band sweeping across the page, and inside it a white rounded panel carrying the notice: "The 2021 examination papers were adjusted to compensate for disruptions to learning due to COVID-19. This examination paper does not necessarily reflect the same structure and format as the examination papers of past or subsequent years." No question content, no data, no diagram.
notes: Cover-page furniture only (page 1). Not bindable to any question card. The stamp box is cut at the top edge, hence truncated.

description: The Question 1(a) plant-identification figure with its surrounding text. At the top: "Answer any seven questions.", "Each question carries 10 marks.", "Question 1", "(a) Identify each of the following plants." Below are three colour photographs side by side, each with a bold capital letter centred above it. A: a single bright yellow flower with five broad glossy petals and a dense cluster of yellow stamens at the centre, growing among deeply divided/lobed green leaves and grass. B: a clump of thistle plants photographed against a dark green background, showing purple-mauve brush-like flowerheads sitting on green globe-shaped heads covered in stiff spines, with spiny winged stems and prickly leaves. C: a low broadleaf plant growing in grass, forming a spreading rosette of large smooth lance-shaped to oval leaves with slightly wavy margins and a prominent pale midrib; a faint photographer credit watermark sits in the bottom-right corner of that photo. Beneath the photographs is a three-row bordered answer table with the printed row labels "A:", "B:" and "C:". The last line, part (b) about annual and biennial lifecycles, runs off the bottom of the crop.
notes: Near-duplicate of p03-i1: identical photographs and answer table, but this crop starts two lines higher (it includes the Section A rubric lines). Either crop carries the full figure; i1 is the tighter one. Only the trailing part (b) sentence is sliced, not the figure. Letters A, B and C are bare identifiers — the paper does not name the plants anywhere, so no meanings are recorded here.

description: The Question 1(a) plant-identification figure, cropped tightly. Heading "Question 1" and "(a) Identify each of the following plants.", then three colour photographs in a row, each captioned with a bold capital letter above it. A: a bright yellow five-petalled glossy flower with a central boss of yellow stamens, among divided green leaves and grass. B: several thistle plants with purple-mauve brush-like flowerheads on green globular spiny heads, spiny stems and prickly leaves, against a dark green background. C: a broadleaf rosette plant in grass with large smooth lance-shaped/oval leaves with wavy margins and a pale prominent midrib, small credit watermark bottom-right. Below is the three-row bordered answer table printed "A:", "B:", "C:". The first words of part (b) appear at the very bottom and are sliced.
notes: Duplicate content of p03-i0 (same three photographs, same lettering, same answer table); this is the tighter crop and is the better one to bind. Figure itself is complete; only the trailing part (b) line is cut.

description: The Question 2 stimulus block. Header line "Question 2   Answer either (a) or (b).", then the article headed "Herbicide resistance confirmed in wild oats" set in three paragraphs of prose about wild oats being a widely recognised weed of Irish tillage fields, control by hand-rogueing, direct drilling, crop rotation and total herbicides, and Teagasc sampling six wild oat field populations that survived a total herbicide. Attribution line "(Adapted from Farmers Journal, 2020)". To the right of the first paragraphs is a colour photograph: a close-up of a person's weathered hands, wearing denim jeans and standing beside a rusty steel machine or trailer in a ripening cereal crop, holding a bunch of grassy panicles whose long drooping stalks carry large pointed oat-like spikelets. The final visible line is "(a) (i) Explain herbicide resistance." with the top of its answer box.
notes: This crop is a prose stimulus with an illustrative photograph; the photo is not itself examined (no identify-the-weed part). Bottom of the crop slices an empty answer box, not any figure content.

description: The Question 2(b) alternative. Centred word "Or", then "(b) A student wanted to investigate the capillarity in both a compacted soil and an uncompacted soil." To the right is a colour photograph of two cupped hands holding a mound of dark crumbly moist soil, with a small green seedling with roughly four broad leaves growing out of the soil, against a dark background. Below are "(i) State a prediction for this investigation." with a two-line answer box and "(ii) Describe a suitable method the student could use to carry out this investigation." with the top of its answer box.
notes: Stock illustrative photograph attached to a practical-investigation question; carries no examinable data. Bottom edge slices an empty answer box only.

description: The Question 3(a) farm safety notice. The sign is a rectangular panel with a dark navy border: a dark blue band across the top carries the white heading "Farm Safety Notice" and a matching dark blue band across the bottom carries "THINK SAFETY FIRST!". Between them are four rows, each with a pictogram on the left and a message panel on the right. Row 1: a red circular prohibition sign (red ring with red diagonal bar) enclosing a black silhouette of a walking pedestrian, beside a red panel with white text "No unauthorised persons allowed beyond this point". Row 2: a yellow warning triangle with a black border enclosing a black silhouette of a horned bovine head in profile, beside a blank yellow panel with a blue outline containing only the bold letter "A". Row 3: a yellow warning triangle enclosing a black silhouette of a tractor, beside a yellow panel with the underlined word "CAUTION" above "Farm machinery in operation". Row 4: a red circular prohibition sign enclosing a black silhouette of an adult figure bent towards a small child, beside a solid red panel containing only the bold white letter "B". To the left of the sign is the question text "(a) The following is an example of a farm safety notice displayed at the entrance to a farm." and "(i) State the meaning of symbols A and B on the sign.", followed by a two-part answer table printed "A:" and "B:". The line "(ii) State the function of C and D." is sliced by the bottom edge.
notes: High-value symbol-identification crop. A and B are deliberately blank message panels — the pictogram beside each is the thing to be decoded (A = the horned-bovine-head warning triangle; B = the adult-and-child prohibition circle). Do NOT copy the two captioned rows ("No unauthorised persons..." and "CAUTION Farm machinery in operation") onto A or B: those captions belong to the other two rows. The figure itself is complete; only the following question line is sliced.

description: The Question 3(a)(ii) equipment figure. Above it the tail of the previous answer box printed "B:", then the line "(ii) State the function of C and D." Below is a bordered two-cell table whose header row reads "C" (left) and "D" (right), each cell containing a product photograph on a white background. C: a long two-handled hand tool; two straight steel handles ending in moulded blue rubber grips, joined by a compound hinge with three riveted pivot plates, driving a heavy head at the far end formed by a large rounded jaw that encloses a circular opening, with a short blade/clamping face on the inner left side. It is a squeeze-operated clamping and crushing tool. D: an assembly of tubular stainless steel — a broad U-shaped frame whose two arms end in black rubber caps, hinged to a long straight ratcheted bar that carries a lever with a D-shaped hand grip at its upper end; a blue cord loop and a red cord loop with hooked ends hang from the ratchet mechanism. Below the photographs is a two-row answer table printed "C:" and "D:", then "(iii) In relation to picture C at part (ii) above, state one advantage of using this piece of equipment to enhance sustainability of the farm." with the top of its answer box.
notes: Both photographs are complete and legible; I also pulled the two embedded source images out of the PDF (829x525 and 828x529) to check the detail at full resolution. C is a heavy squeeze-clamp tool with a ring-shaped jaw; D is a ratcheted frame with two coloured cords, i.e. an obstetric/traction frame. I have deliberately not named either tool in the description — that identification is the scheme's job. Top edge slices the previous answer box, bottom edge slices an empty answer box; neither is figure content.

description: The Question 3(b)(i) farm-machinery identification figure. Centred word "Or" at the top, then "(b) (i) Identify the farm machines, labelled A and B, which are attached to each tractor." Two colour photographs sit side by side, each with a thick red downward arrow (blue outline) pointing at the implement, and a bold capital letter above the arrow. A: a crawler tractor running on rubber tracks instead of rear wheels, working across bare brown cultivated soil under a blue cloudy sky, towing a large orange implement — a tall hopper/tank with the manufacturer's name on its side, from which a bank of flexible delivery pipes runs down and back to a wide rear frame carrying a long row of tine/coulter units with small press wheels; the red arrow labelled A points at the orange hopper unit. B: a green grass field, with the rear wheel and drawbar of a tractor visible at the right, towing a red trailed wagon on a tandem twin-wheel axle; the wagon has high mesh sides and is loaded with green cut grass, with a yellow rotor/beater at the top of the body and a yellow pick-up/mowing header slung at the front bottom of the wagon cutting the standing grass; the red arrow labelled B points at the top of the wagon body. Below is a two-row answer table printed "A:" and "B:", then "(ii) The tractor in picture A is fitted with two tracks instead of four wheels. Suggest one advantage of using a tractor fitted with tracks." with the top of its answer box.
notes: High-value machinery-identification crop; both photographs and both red pointer arrows are fully inside the crop (I checked the PDF image boxes: the right-hand photo ends about 34 px inside the crop edge). Letters A and B are bare identifiers, so no meanings recorded. Bottom slices an empty answer box only.

description: The Question 4 farm-layout photograph, with heading "Question 4" and "Study the photograph of the farm layout below and answer the questions which follow." The image is an oblique aerial (drone) colour photograph of an Irish farmyard set in bright green grass fields with mature trees and hedgerows along the boundaries. In the foreground stands a large modern shed with a dark green roof carrying two long rows of translucent roof lights, on a pale concrete apron. Behind it are a curved (arched) grey-roofed shed, a wide low grey/green roofed range of older sheds, and several smaller green-roofed buildings; open tanks/channels and a concrete yard lie between them. At the top left a white dwelling house with a grey roof sits beside a tarred entrance road with several parked cars, and a tractor is parked among the buildings. At the top right a large black plastic-covered silage pit weighted with tyres sits beside the trees. On the right-hand side of the yard is a pyramid stack of about twenty pink/white wrapped round bales, a line of parked machinery and implements (including a red machine and a trailer) on bare stony ground, and gravel roadways loop around the yard between the buildings and the fields. Below the photograph the line "(a) Identify one way in which the farm in the photograph could become more energy efficient." with the top of its answer box.
notes: The whole aerial photograph is inside the crop (grass and roadway are visible along its bottom edge before the text resumes). No letters or annotations on the image — parts (a), (b), (c) all reason from the photograph as a whole.

description: The Question 6(a)(i) tick-box item. Header "Question 6   Answer either (a) or (b).", then "(a) (i) Identify the part of the plant where respiration takes place by placing a tick in the correct box." Below is a small two-column table: the left column has three pale green cells reading, top to bottom, "Ribosome", "Mitochondria" and "Chloroplast"; the right column has three empty white boxes for the tick. To the right of the text is a colour photograph of a single small seedling with two yellow-green leaves and a folded shoot tip emerging from a mound of dark crumbly soil, with blurred green grass and sunbeams behind. Below, "(ii) Outline two ways in which a farmer can increase airflow through soil to allow for increased respiration in the rhizosphere." with a numbered answer box ("1.") whose second row is sliced by the bottom edge.
notes: The only figure-like content is the three-option tick table, which is complete and legible; the seedling photograph is decorative stock. Bottom edge slices an empty answer box only.

description: The Question 10 stem. Heading "Question 10" and the prose "The Murphy family operate one of Ireland's sheep dairy farms in Co. Galway. They produce artisan products for a niche market. Their produce is available in approximately 50 shops and in some of Ireland's top restaurants." To the right is a colour photograph taken inside a sheep milking parlour: several ewes with cream-coloured fleeces stand side by side in a row, seen from behind, restrained between galvanised steel rails and dark backing boards, with teat cups and clear milk tubing attached to their udders and milk lines running along the parlour; the ewe on the left carries a red raddle or spray mark on her rump, and the floor is wet concrete. Below the photograph is "(a) Distinguish between artisan produce and a niche market." with a four-row answer box, the last row sliced by the bottom edge.
notes: Important gap for the later wave: the sheep-milk composition PIE CHART used at Q10(c) (Water 84%, Protein 4%, Fat 7%, Lactose 5%) is NOT in this crop and has no crop of its own — it is drawn as vector chart objects in the PDF, so the extractor never rasterised it. If a Q10(c) card needs the chart it must be re-rendered from page 15 of the PDF. The photograph here is illustrative only.

description: The Question 12 stem. Heading "Question 12" and the prose "The manager of a 250 sow integrated pig unit was alerted that some of his young bonhams (piglets) were ill. On inspection of the bonhams, he noticed that they were breathing quickly, weak, had a scour and their skin was pale." To the right is a colour photograph of four young pink piglets standing close together facing the camera in a pen, with pale blue penning rails and a bright indoor background behind them. Below are "(a) Identify the disease that the bonhams are suffering from based on all of the symptoms described above." with a single-line answer box, and "(b) State the cause of the identified disease." with the top of its answer box.
notes: Prose stem with an illustrative photograph of piglets; the photograph carries no diagnostic detail (no visible lesions or symptoms), so it must not be presented as evidence for the diagnosis. Bottom edge slices an empty answer box.

description: The Question 13(a) stimulus article, boxed. Blue heading "UCD trials indicate increased ewe milk production and lamb weight gain in flocks grazing multi-species swards", then two paragraphs defining multi-species swards as a mixture of two or more species consisting of grasses (perennial ryegrass, timothy), herbs (chicory, plantain) and legumes (white and red clover), and setting out the challenges — persistency of the herbs and legumes, the impossibility of blanket post-emergence herbicide, and difficult autumn establishment. Inside the box at the right is a colour photograph taken from a low angle in a lush green sward: tall grass leaves and a seed head fill the foreground, a single ewe with a green marking on her back stands looking at the camera in the middle distance, with more sheep, a fence line and a distant hedgerow under a blue sky with white clouds behind. Attribution "(Adapted from Irish Independent, 2020)". Below, "(i) Identify one plant named in the article that can fix atmospheric nitrogen." with its answer box; the start of part (ii) is sliced at the bottom.
notes: Article stimulus with an illustrative sward photograph; nothing in the photograph is examined (species are named in the prose, not identified from the image). The article box and photo are both complete.

description: The Question 14(b)(i) breed-identification figure. Line "(b) (i) Identify each of the following cattle and sheep breeds." then four colour photographs in a row, each with a bold capital letter above it. A: a heavy blocky sheep standing side-on in grass with a dense creamy-white fleece, an entirely black wool-free face and black ears, and black legs, with a wire fence and green foliage behind. B: a beef bull standing side-on in grass, deep dark red-brown with heavy roan/white flecking through the coat over the shoulders and ribs, thick curly coat, broad head with short pale upturned horns, wearing a leather halter with a lead rein held from off-camera, clipped hedge behind. C: an extremely heavily muscled beef bull, white coated with large irregular blue-grey and black patches, with pronounced double-muscled hindquarters and shoulders and black lower legs, wearing a halter with a rosette/prize card at its head, standing on show-ground grass with railings and spectators behind. D: a compact meaty sheep standing side-on in grass, short creamy-tan fleece, a bare white face with a dark nose and white ears held out sideways, and bare white legs, with a tree trunk and dark foliage behind. Below the photographs is a four-row bordered answer table printed "A:", "B:", "C:" and "D:". The start of part (ii) is sliced at the very bottom.
notes: Highest-value crop type in this subject, but flagged truncated: photograph D runs off the RIGHT edge of the crop — checking the PDF image boxes, roughly the last 13 px (about 5% of its width, background trees and fence only) is missing. All four animals, all four letters and the whole answer table are fully visible, so the identifying content is intact, but a re-crop of the page-27 region is preferable before binding. Pixel-identical to p27-i1 over their shared area.

description: The Question 14(b)(i) breed-identification figure, identical framing to p27-i0. Line "(b) (i) Identify each of the following cattle and sheep breeds." then four lettered colour photographs: A, a blocky sheep with a creamy-white fleece, a completely black bare face and ears and black legs, standing in grass by a wire fence; B, a beef bull with a deep dark red-brown coat heavily flecked with white/roan hair, a curly coat, a broad head with short upturned horns and a leather halter with a lead rein, standing in front of a hedge; C, a very heavily muscled beef bull, white with large irregular blue-grey and black patches, double-muscled hindquarters, black lower legs and a rosette at the halter, on show-ground grass with railings and spectators behind; D, a compact meaty sheep with a short creamy-tan fleece, a bare white face with a dark nose and outward-held white ears, and bare white legs, in front of a tree. Below is the four-row answer table printed "A:", "B:", "C:" and "D:", with the start of part (ii) sliced at the bottom.
notes: Exact duplicate of p27-i0 — a pixel-for-pixel difference test over the shared 979x519 area returned no differences; this file is just 2 px taller. It carries the same defect: photograph D is clipped at the right edge (about 5% of its background). Bind only one of the two, and preferably re-crop from the PDF.

description: An overlapping fragment of the Question 14(c) Beef HealthCheck material. The top third shows the last rows of the two-column scoring key: a sliced row above, then a navy rounded tile "4" with "Liver other: Liver damage due to other causes, e.g. tumours." on the left and a matching navy "4" tile with "Lung other: Lung damage due to other causes, e.g. abscess or tumour." on the right, then a red tile "5" with "Liver abscess: may occur following gut damage from a high grain diet or as an infection from a 'navel ill' or other infection." (there is no score 5 in the lung column). Below it the animal data table begins: a pale blue title bar "Beef HealthCheck Report", then a purple header row with white text "Tag | Sex | Age (months) | Carcase (kg)", a black-filled header cell "Liver Score" and a grey header cell "Lung Score". Visible data rows: IE 1234567-8-0001, E, 20, 330, liver 1 on green, lung 3 on red; IE 1234567-8-0002, C, 22, 360, liver "3 / 5" on red, lung 1 on green; IE 1234567-8-0003, D, 40, 400, liver 2 on amber, lung 1 on green. The fourth row (IE 1234567-8-0004, B, 44, 500) is sliced through by the bottom edge and rows 0005 to 0007 are missing.
notes: Unusable as a standalone figure: the score key is cut at the top (scores 1-3 missing) and the animal table is cut after three and a half rows of seven. Critical hazard for the later wave — the letters E, C, D and B in the Sex column are animal-category codes, and the key that decodes them ("A = young bull, B = bull, C = steer, D = cow, E = heifer") is printed BELOW the table on page 28 and appears in NO crop. A card using any of these letters must carry that key from the paper. Overlaps p28-i1, i2 and i3.

description: The Question 14(c) Beef HealthCheck scoring key, upper portion. A pale blue title bar reads "Beef HealthCheck Report"; beneath it two side-by-side columns headed "Liver results" and "Lung Results", each with the sub-line "Liver lesions result in reduced performance" / "Lung lesions result in reduced performance" and a grey "Score" column. Rows, each with a coloured rounded score tile on the left of its text: green "1" — "Normal liver: No liver abnormalities detected." and "Normal lung: No lung abnormalities detected."; amber "2" — "Liver damage by fluke but no live fluke: Fluke may not be observed because the animal was (i) treated and cured, (ii) has undergone 'self-cure' or (iii) live fluke may have been present but not observed." and "Limited lung damage: This animal had limited lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection)."; red "3" — "Liver damage by fluke and live fluke: Fluke may be present because the animal was (i) not treated, (ii) re-infected after a previous treatment, (iii) treated with a product that only kills adult fluke, leaving young fluke alive, (iv) given a product to which the fluke have become resistant." and "Extensive lung damage: This animal had extensive lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection)." The navy "4" row ("Liver other" / "Lung other") begins at the bottom and is sliced through the middle of its text; the red "5" liver-abscess row is not present.
notes: Best of the four page-28 fragments for the scoring key (it alone carries the title bar and scores 1-3 in full), but still truncated: score 4 is sliced and score 5 is missing entirely, and the seven-animal data table is absent. Overlaps p28-i0, i2 and i3. No letters on this fragment — the 1 to 5 tiles are score values, not part labels.

description: A shorter fragment of the same Question 14(c) scoring key, starting one line lower than p28-i1 so the "Beef HealthCheck Report" title bar is absent. The top line reads "Liver lesions result in reduced performance" on the left and "Lung lesions result in reduced performance" on the right, each column with a grey "Score" cell beneath. Then: green tile "1" — "Normal liver: No liver abnormalities detected." and "Normal lung: No lung abnormalities detected."; amber tile "2" — "Liver damage by fluke but no live fluke: Fluke may not be observed because the animal was (i) treated and cured, (ii) has undergone 'self-cure' or (iii) live fluke may have been present but not observed." and "Limited lung damage: This animal had limited lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection)."; red tile "3" — "Liver damage by fluke and live fluke..." with its four reasons, and "Extensive lung damage: This animal had extensive lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection)." The last line of the score 3 liver text is sliced by the bottom edge; scores 4 and 5 and the whole animal data table are missing.
notes: Strictly worse than p28-i1 — same key, no title bar, and cut earlier (mid score-3 text). Duplicate/overlapping fragment; do not bind.

description: The lower overlapping fragment of the Question 14(c) material. At the top, the tail of the score-3 liver text ("...young fluke alive, (iv) given a product to which the fluke have become resistant.") is sliced by the upper edge; then the navy "4" tiles with "Liver other: Liver damage due to other causes, e.g. tumours." and "Lung other: Lung damage due to other causes, e.g. abscess or tumour.", and the red "5" tile with "Liver abscess: may occur following gut damage from a high grain diet or as an infection from a 'navel ill' or other infection." Below is the animal data table: pale blue title "Beef HealthCheck Report", purple header row "Tag | Sex | Age (months) | Carcase (kg)" with a black "Liver Score" header and a grey "Lung Score" header, and five data rows — IE 1234567-8-0001, E, 20, 330, liver 1 (green), lung 3 (red); IE 1234567-8-0002, C, 22, 360, liver "3 / 5" (red), lung 1 (green); IE 1234567-8-0003, D, 40, 400, liver 2 (amber), lung 1 (green); IE 1234567-8-0004, B, 44, 500, liver 1 (green), lung 2 (amber); IE 1234567-8-0005, E, 19, 340, liver 3 (red), lung 1 (green). The bottom edge cuts immediately below row 0005.
notes: The most complete of the four page-28 fragments for the data table, but still truncated: rows IE 1234567-8-0006 (C, 20, 350, liver 2, lung 4) and IE 1234567-8-0007 (D, 56, 410, liver 4, lung 1) are below the crop, and score tiles 1-3 of the key are above it. Part (c)(iii) asks about all seven animals, so this crop cannot support that part. Same decoding hazard as p28-i0: the Sex letters E, C, D, B appear without the "A = young bull, B = bull, C = steer, D = cow, E = heifer" key, which is printed under the table on page 28 and is in no crop.

description: The Question 15(a) stem. Heading "Question 15" and the prose "A student carried out an investigation to compare how application rates and source of organic fertiliser in autumn will affect grass dry matter (DM), earthworm population and spring soil nutrient availability in the hope of increasing food production, in-line with Foodwise 2025." To the right is a wide colour banner image — the Food Wise 2025 report cover: a sunset over the sea seen from a grassy clifftop headland, with a girl in a pink t-shirt and denim shorts sitting on a wooden post-and-rail fence with her back to the camera, and four black-and-white cows grazing on the grass behind her. Along the bottom of the banner are the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine harp crest with "Agriculture, Food and the Marine / Talmhaíochta, Bia agus Mara" at the left, and at the right the words "LOCAL ROOTS GLOBAL REACH", the large title "Food Wise 2025" and the strapline "A 10-year vision for the Irish agri-food industry". Below are "(i) State a hypothesis for this investigation." with a two-row answer box and "(ii) Identify the independent and dependent variables in this investigation." with the top of its box.
notes: The banner is a policy-document cover used as decoration; it carries no data. Gap to record for the later wave: the Q15(b) results GRAPH on page 33 (total available kg DM/ha, November to March, for control, slurry low 22,000 l/ha, slurry high 33,000 l/ha, farmyard manure low 12 t/ha and farmyard manure high 25 t/ha) has NO crop at all — it is vector-drawn in the PDF and was never rasterised, so a Q15(b) card must re-render page 33.

description: The Question 16(a) milk-payment table, partially captured. Header "Question 16   Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d)." and the stem "(a) Two dairy farmers (Dan and Joe) are comparing the amount of money they are getting paid for their milk. Analyse the data in the table and answer the questions which follow." To the right is a small colour photograph of milk being poured from a white jug into a graduated glass laboratory beaker standing on a grey bench, with a blurred grey background. The table below has two green-shaded column headers, "Dan" and "Joe". Row "Supply (litres, kg)": 50,000 L (51,500 kg) for both. The blue-shaded block "Protein" carries the printed note "A = €5.48 / kg" and three data rows: 3.5 % and 3.3 %; 1,803 kg and 1,700 kg; then a bright yellow cell containing "?" for Dan and a peach cell containing "€9,316" for Joe. The blue-shaded "Fat" block follows with rows 4.45 % and 3.96 %, then 2,292 kg and 2,039 kg. The bottom edge of the crop slices horizontally through the printed note "B = €3.35 / kg" (only the tops of the characters survive) and cuts off the rest of the Fat block and the whole "Processing cost deduction / C = €0.04 / litre / €2,000 / €2,000" row.

labelMeanings.meaning: printed in the table's Protein block as "A = €5.48 / kg" — the price per kg of protein
printed in the table's Fat block as "B = €3.35 / kg" — the price per kg of fat; sliced by the bottom edge of this crop so only the tops of the characters are visible

notes: Truncated and NOT safe to bind: the Fat block is incomplete, label B is sliced, and the third label C ("C = €0.04 / litre", the processing cost deduction) plus the €2,000 deductions are entirely missing — a student cannot do the (i) calculation from this crop. Re-crop page 35. Also note the Q16(a)(iii) milk-quality table (TBC 75,000 cfu/ml, SCC 320,000 cells/ml with the creamery advice) on page 36 has no crop of its own.

description: The Question 16(c) stimulus, boxed. The line introducing the article is sliced along the top edge of the crop ("Read the article on 'Sustainable Dairy Production in Europe' and answer the questions which follow." — the first line's lower halves only). Inside the box is the blue heading "Sustainable Dairy Production in Europe" and two paragraphs: the EU's top priorities of at least a 40% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from 1990 levels, a 27% improvement in energy efficiency and a 27% share of renewable energy by 2030; and the Irish dairy sector's commitment while exporting to over 155 countries. At the left of the box is a colour photograph of two black-and-white dairy cows walking in a green paddock; each cow carries a padded box-shaped pack strapped over her back with a girth strap around the barrel, with red flexible tubing running from the pack forward over the shoulder to the head, and wears a coloured neck collar/halter and yellow ear tags; a stone wall and trees are behind. Attribution "(Adapted from Sustainable Dairy in Europe, 2019)". Below, "(i) Outline how the European Union would achieve their top priorities." with the top rows of its answer box.
notes: Article stimulus; the article box and photograph are both complete (only the introductory question line above the box is sliced). The cows' back-mounted equipment is visible but unlabelled and is not examined — do not caption it with a device name.

description: The Question 16(d) virtual fencing item. Centred "Or", then "(d) The application of technology in Agriculture is increasing. Virtual fencing (VF) is one such technology; it enables the confinement or movement of animals without the use of fixed fencing. The VF system requires that the animals wear a Global Positioning System (GPS) collar which emits an audio warning when the animals approach the VF boundaries." To the right is an annotated colour photograph of a green grazing paddock with trees along the far boundary: a single white/light-roan cow stands grazing head-down in the middle ground, two thin white marker posts stand in the field, and three pale-green rounded label boxes are overlaid on the image. A thin white line is drawn diagonally across the field behind the cow; the label "No fence boundary" sits on it at the top right and the label "Potential electric shock" sits on it at the upper left. description: The Question 18(c) lactation graph, complete. The line "(c) Analyse the graph showing the lactation period of a dairy cow and answer the questions which follow." sits above a schematic curve diagram that has NO numbered axes and no units — time runs left to right, energy runs bottom to top. Two curves run across the chart: a dark green curve labelled "Energy requirement" (label in green just after the peak) and a second curve that is dark maroon-red where it lies below the green curve and blue where it lies above it, labelled "Energy intake" (blue label in a box at the left). Both dip slightly, then rise steeply to a peak and fall away to the right. Between the two curves in the rising/peak phase is a bright yellow filled area carrying a diagonal orange banner with the words "Negative Energy Balance"; after the two curves cross (marked by a maroon dashed vertical line) the intake curve lies above the requirement curve and the gap is filled pale blue-green with a diagonal banner reading "Excess energy". A black square-dotted vertical line near the left of centre is captioned "Calving" at the top; a yellow square-dotted vertical line at the right is captioned "Drying off" at the top; two further yellow dotted verticals bracket an orange horizontal bar low in the plot labelled "Transition phase", which straddles calving. A thick red double-headed horizontal arrow labelled "Challenging period" runs from calving to the maroon dashed crossing line. Pale yellow vertical bands shade the far left of the chart and the region to the right of drying off. Along the bottom is a blue banner divided into four labelled stages, left to right: "Dry phase", "Early lactation", "Mid lactation", "Late lactation", with a lighter blue unlabelled segment at the far right. Attribution "(Adapted from Shauman, 2015)". Below the graph, "(i) Explain what is the drying off period." with its answer box and "(ii) Outline one reason for the negative energy balance in early lactation." with the top of its box.

description: A strip taken from the front cover of the paper. A pale blue curved band runs across the width of the page. description: A page region covering the top of Section A and Question 1 part (a): the printed lines Answer any seven questions, Each question carries 10 marks, Question 1, Answer either (a) or (b), and the instruction Identify each of the following plants by placing a tick in the correct box. Its options are Wheat, Barley, Linseed, Oats. Photograph (iii) is a close-up of dense green three-lobed leaves covered in water droplets with a single white globe-shaped flower head at the lower left; only the first two of its four options, Plantain and Clover, appear before the crop ends.
notes: The three photographs are keyed by the question part numbers (i), (ii), (iii), not by letters, so lettersVisible is empty. Bottom edge cuts through photograph (iii) and through the Clover tick box, and the Dandelion and Chicory rows are missing entirely, so this crop must not be bound on its own for part (iii). description: Question 1 part (b)(i), headed Or and Identify each of the following plants commonly found in grassland. description: Question 12 part (a), headed The photographs show some common breeds of cattle and sheep. Identify each breed using the list of names and write your answer in the space provided. Four colour photographs are arranged two by two, each with a bold letter centred above it. A is a side-on photograph of a heavily muscled cream-white bull with a short curly forelock, wearing a black leather halter with a lead rope, standing on green grass with a stone wall and grey sky behind. B is a side-on photograph of a heavily muscled deep golden-red / russet-brown bull with a paler ring around the muzzle, also wearing a black halter with a pink lead rope, standing on grass in front of bare winter trees and a wire fence. description: Question 13 part (a) stimulus. Below the heading Question 13 and the instruction Read the following article on liver fluke and answer the questions which follow is a boxed newspaper-style article whose text reads: Liver fluke thrive in the Irish wet climate. It is estimated to cost Irish farmers over 90 million euro annually. It is an issue in both cattle and sheep, but sheep are often the most badly affected. It affects all ages of sheep as it is picked up off the grass when sheep are grazing. This commonly occurs in the autumn and winter months. Set into the right side of the same box is a portrait colour photograph on a black background of a single liver fluke: a flat, leaf-shaped (lanceolate) parasitic flatworm, orange-brown and translucent, with a narrow cone-shaped anterior end at the top, a broad rounded body, and a dark branching internal pattern visible down its midline. Beneath the box in italics is the source line (Adapted from Teagasc, 2020), then part (i), Identify the estimated cost of liver fluke to Irish farmers annually, with a blank answer box, and part (ii), Outline one environmental condition that allows liver fluke to thrive.
notes: Mixed crop: the examinable content is the boxed article prose (the 90 million euro figure answers part (i) and the wet climate answers part (ii)); the liver fluke photograph beside it is a genuine specimen photograph but is illustrative - no part of the question asks about it. Both the article and the photograph are complete and legible. Truncated is true because the top crop edge slices a line of text above Question 13 and the bottom edge slices the part (ii) answer box.  [Adjudicated: figure intact. Cut at the boundary: A stripped remnant of the previous line of prose along the top edge, and the part (ii) answer box at the bottom edge.]

description: A page region of Question 17 part (a). The printed stem reads: A student was asked to investigate the effect of temperature on the percentage germination of certified grass seeds (with germination and certified grass seeds underlined). The student conducted the investigation at five set temperatures (15 degrees C, 20, 25, 30 and 35 degrees C). At each temperature 100 seeds were sown. The student repeated the investigation four times and calculated the mean (average) percentage germination. To the right of the first lines is a landscape colour photograph, taken close to ground level, of many fine pale-green grass seedlings just emerging from dark crumbly compost, with a green tray rim visible along the top of the shot. Below the stem is part (i), Explain the underlined terms, and the top of the answer grid whose first row reads Germination:.
notes: Classified decorative: the photograph of germinating grass seedlings is generic stock illustration, is never referred to by the question, and carries no data, apparatus or labels. The examinable content of Q17(a) is entirely in the prose (five temperatures, 100 seeds, four repeats). Photograph is whole; the crop edge slices only the blank answer grid.

description: Question 17 part (b)(i), the graph-completion item. The instruction above reads: The percentage germination of the grass seeds at 15 degrees C and 25 degrees C are already plotted on the graph. Complete the graph below by plotting the percentage germination of the grass seeds at 20 degrees C as calculated at part (a) and at 30 degrees C. The figure is a partly-completed bar chart on a pale blue gradient panel, titled in red Effect of Temperature on the Germination % of Grass Seeds. The vertical axis is labelled % Germination and is scaled 0 to 85 in steps of 5 with horizontal gridlines at every step. The horizontal axis is labelled Temperature (oC) with five category positions: 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35. Three black bars are already drawn, each with its value printed in white inside the top of the bar: a short bar of 15 at 15 degrees C, a tall bar of 80 at 25 degrees C, and a bar of 35 at 35 degrees C. The 20 degrees C and 30 degrees C positions are deliberately empty for the student to plot. Beneath the chart is a results table with two rows: the header row Temperature (oC) with entries 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and the row % Germination with entries 15, then a yellow-highlighted cell reading Calculated at part (a) for the 20 degrees C column, then 80, 65 and 35. Below the table is part (ii), State one piece of advice you would give to farmers on the sowing of grass seed based on your conclusion and also supported by the results of this investigation.
notes: Note the deliberate incompleteness: this is a plot-the-missing-bars task, so the empty 20 and 30 degrees C positions are correct as printed and must not be described as damage. The value for 20 degrees C comes from part (a)(v) (the four trial counts 62, 59, 61, 58 out of 100 seeds); the value for 30 degrees C is given in the table as 65. Axes, gridlines, all three plotted values and the whole table are legible; the crop edge slices only the part (ii) answer box.  [Adjudicated: figure intact. Cut at the boundary: The preceding stem line ("The table and graph below show the results obtained by the student.") sits above the crop, and the part (ii) answer box is sliced at the bottom edge.]

description: A page region of Question 18 part (a)(iii). The text reads: Farmers are increasingly using Global Positioning Systems (GPS) when spreading chemical fertiliser on the land. Below the photographs is a four-row answer grid numbered 1. and 2.
notes: The two photographs are contextual illustration of the technology named in the stem - the question asks for advantages of GPS, not for identification of the machinery - so a card can show them but does not need them. description: The Question 9(b) stimulus article in a bordered box. Instruction line above: '(b) Read the article on the SEASOLUTIONS Project and answer the questions which follow.' The box has a pale green banner headed 'SEASOLUTIONS PROJECT'. The justified body text reads: 'Reducing methane emissions from ruminants is one of the biggest challenges to face the agricultural sector in the last decade. The SEASOLUTIONS Project is committed to making a positive impact on methane emissions in agriculture. By using seaweeds and seaweed derived ingredients to positively affect the rumen and rumen microbiota to reduce methane emissions and improve ruminant health. By adding seaweed components to the feed of sheep and cattle indoors on high grain based diets, Irish researchers have reduced methane production by 20%. A critical aspect of this project is to test such seaweed supplements within the context of a pasture-based production system.' Set into the right of the text block is a colour photograph of black-and-white cattle grazing lush green grass under a blue sky with white clouds; the nearest animal is head-down grazing with a yellow ear tag visible, and a red-and-white animal stands behind. description: The Question 14(d) faecal egg count data, presented as two small tables beside a montage of microscope images. Stem above: '(d) A faecal egg count (FEC) is used to monitor parasite numbers in sheep. It is carried out regularly throughout the grass growing season. Jim took dung samples from each of his 3 flocks and sent it for analysis. The following are the results.' First table, headed by a pale blue cell reading 'Jim's Samples' and a row label 'FEC (eggs per gram)', has three pale green column headings Flock 1, Flock 2, Flock 3 with the values 430, 220 and 790. To the right is a montage of six photomicrographs in a two-column by three-row grid, each a bright-field microscope view of a stained faecal smear in mauve, olive and pale blue tones. Top left: a single small dark brown ovoid body on an almost empty lilac field. Top right: two large pale-rimmed oval eggs each containing a dark granular mass, with plant debris beneath. Middle left, marked with a small dark letter C in the top left corner: a mauve field with plant fragments and a large brown wedge of debris at lower left. Middle right, marked D: a single elongated oval egg with a thick clear shell containing granular contents, on an olive field. Bottom left, marked E: two dark orange-brown lemon-shaped eggs among pale fibrous plant material. Bottom right, marked F: two small pale olive ovoid eggs among plant debris on a blue-grey field. Below the tables, '(i) Briefly describe the dosing plan Jim would carry out in flocks 1 and 2.' with an answer table showing 'Flock 1:' and 'Flock 2:'.
notes: WARNING for any card built from this crop. The letters C, D, E and F belong to the ORIGINAL published photomicrograph montage (acknowledgements credit page 26 to researchgate.net); no part of Q14(d) refers to them and there is nothing in the paper that decodes them. Worse, the two top-row panels carry no visible letters at all - I zoomed in at 7x to check and confirmed the A and B labels are absent - so the lettering is incomplete and inconsistent. Do NOT present these letters to a student. If the crop is used, re-crop to the two data tables only. The tables themselves are complete and clean; truncated flagged true for the sliced answer table at the bottom edge and because of the unresolvable partial lettering on the montage.  [Adjudicated: FIGURE CUT — The tops of the two top-row photomicrograph panels, and with them the panel labels A and B — those two panels are visibly shorter than the C/D and E/F rows and carry no letter where C, D, E and F each carry one.]

Left, pointing to Pedometer: 'Measures increase in walking activity at oestrus'. description: The Question 17(b) plant breeding selection diagram. Stem above: '(b) Plant breeding is the science of changing the traits of plants in order to produce desired characteristics in a direction favourable to peoples' needs. Scientists work on selecting the high yielding plants and breeding these.' The diagram runs left to right in three stages. Stage one, a graph drawn with thick blue axes: the vertical axis is labelled 'Yield' and the horizontal axis carries the two bold endpoint labels 'Low' at the left and 'High' at the right; neither axis has a numerical scale, tick marks or units. A blue symmetrical bell-shaped curve rises and falls across it with a blue dashed vertical line dropped from its peak. A magenta circle rings the right-hand tail of the curve where it meets the axis, marking the high end of the distribution. A magenta arrow leads from that circle rightwards to stage two: a stylised clip-art illustration of a clump of bright green blade-like leaves with about eight small orange dots scattered above and among them, representing seed or grain. A second magenta arrow leads on to stage three, a second graph with the same thick blue axes, vertical axis labelled 'Yield' and horizontal endpoints 'Low' and 'High'. This graph shows the original curve redrawn in pale blue with its dashed peak line, plus a new magenta curve of similar shape shifted to the right with its own dashed peak line, so the two peaks sit side by side with the magenta one further towards 'High'. Below the diagram, '(i) Outline two reasons why scientists select the plants with the highest yield for breeding.' and a ruled answer table beginning at '1.'
notes: A complete and bindable diagram showing selection shifting a population distribution towards higher yield. Important accuracy caveat for a card writer: as printed, the VERTICAL axis is labelled 'Yield' and the HORIZONTAL axis is labelled only 'Low' to 'High' - there are no units and no numeric scale on either axis, and the labelling is arguably unconventional (a frequency distribution would normally put yield on the horizontal axis). Describe the axes exactly as printed rather than 'correcting' them. Truncated flagged true only for the blank answer table sliced at the bottom edge; the diagram itself is whole.  [Adjudicated: figure intact. Cut at the boundary: The first blank answer box under part (b)(i), at the bottom edge.]

description: The Question 17(d) stimulus article in a thin bordered box. Instruction above: '(d) Read the article and answer the questions which follow.' Blue bold headline: 'UK decides to push towards gene editing technologies'. Body text in two paragraphs: 'The British government outlined new plans to unlock the power of gene editing (GE) as a suite of tools to help farmers grow more resistant, nutritious and productive crops.' and 'GE makes plant breeding faster, more precise and more efficient, with the aim to produce new varieties that are more nutritious, more resistant to pests, diseases and viruses, more productive and carry traits that are more beneficial to the environment.' Set into the right of the text block is a colour illustration of a DNA double helix rendered as two twisted copper-brown strands with rungs between them, with a pair of fine metal tweezers held by a human hand reaching in from the right to lift out one red-highlighted rung, against a soft blue-and-white background. Right-aligned italic attribution below the box: '(Adapted from Irish Farmers Journal, 2021)'. Below, '(i) Briefly explain the principles of gene editing.' with a blank ruled answer box beginning.
notes: Classified 'text' because the examinable stimulus is entirely prose that can be typed out; the DNA illustration is decorative and is not referenced by either part of Q17(d). The article box and its attribution are complete. Bottom edge slices the blank answer box.

The diagram is a flower or petal arrangement of nine overlapping circles, all labelled in white text. At the centre, a lime-green circle reading 'Food Safety'. Around it, eight circles alternating between mid-teal and dark teal. Reading clockwise from the top: 'Energy & Emission' (dark teal, top); 'Animal Welfare' (mid teal, upper right); 'Socio-economic' (dark teal, right); 'Animal Health' (mid teal, lower right); 'Water' (dark teal, bottom); 'Health & Safety' (mid teal, lower left); 'Biodiversity' (dark teal, left); 'Traceability' (mid teal, upper left). The four mid-teal circles sit in the diagonal positions and overlap the central Food Safety circle; the four dark teal circles sit at the top, bottom, left and right and sit behind them. Italic attribution to the lower right of the diagram: '(Adapted from origingreen.ie, 2021)'. Below, '(i) Briefly describe how each of the following key components relate to food safety.' with answer boxes headed 'Animal Welfare:' and 'Health and Safety:'.

description: The complete 'Integrated Management System' weed control figure for Question 18(b). Stem above: '(b) The diagram below shows an Integrated Management System for controlling weeds.' and 'Analyse the diagram and answer the questions which follow.' The figure has two halves inside one outer border. LEFT: a table with a peach-coloured header cell reading 'Examples of Cultural Control Options' above nine single-column rows listing, from top to bottom: Increased seed rates; Cover crops; Competitive crops; Roguing; Crop rotation; Whole cropping; Crop destruction; On-farm hygiene; Machinery hygiene. RIGHT: a pale blue panel containing two stacked triangles. The upper one is captioned 'The Past' in a pale green banner and is an INVERTED grey triangle divided into three horizontal bands, widest at the top: 'Post-emergence' (widest band, at the top), 'Pre-emergence' (middle band) and 'Cultural Control' (narrowest band, at the point). Two thick red arrows point inward and down at this inverted triangle from either side. A thick blue arrow points straight down from it to the lower diagram. The lower one is captioned 'The Future' in a pale green banner and is an UPRIGHT green triangle divided into three horizontal bands, widest at the base: 'Post - emergence' (narrowest band, at the apex), 'Pre-emergence' (middle band) and 'Cultural Control' (widest band, at the base). Two thick red arrows point outward and down away from this triangle on either side. Right-aligned italic attribution beneath: '(Adapted from Teagasc, 2021)'. Below, '(i) Explain pre-emergence weed control.' with a three-line blank ruled answer box.

labelMeanings.meaning: The inverted grey triangle - Post-emergence control is the widest band at the top, Pre-emergence is the middle band, Cultural Control is the narrowest band at the point
The upright green triangle - Post-emergence control is the narrowest band at the apex, Pre-emergence is the middle band, Cultural Control is the widest band at the base
Increased seed rates; Cover crops; Competitive crops; Roguing; Crop rotation; Whole cropping; Crop destruction; On-farm hygiene; Machinery hygiene

notes: Fully intact and one of the best figures in the paper - table, both triangles, all band labels, both sets of red arrows and the attribution are all inside the crop. The teaching point Q18(b)(ii) turns on is the inversion between the two triangles: reliance moves away from post-emergence chemistry towards cultural control. description: Two colour photographs of farm machinery side by side, each tagged by a thick red arrow drawn onto the photo pointing at the implement. Left photograph, arrow labelled A: a tractor (green cab, black bodywork, yellow wheel rims, driver in the cab) viewed from behind in a green grass field, carrying a rear three-point-linkage-mounted hopper machine — a wide teal-blue hopper with a red lid that tapers downwards to two outlets over a red frame; the hopper carries a white 'SULKY' decal. The shape and brand are those of a twin-disc fertiliser spreader, though no discs are clearly resolvable at this resolution. Right photograph, arrow labelled B: a large green single-axle tanker with a wide flotation tyre standing on a concrete yard in front of a dark conifer hedge; a white manufacturer decal on the barrel (partly legible, ending in '...Technology') and a small model number. Folded upright at the rear of the tanker is a tall vertical boom carrying a dense stack of green flexible hoses ending in black outlet shoes — a trailing shoe / dribble bar slurry applicator in the transport position; a second stack of hoses lies folded at the bottom. Below the photographs the question text '(a) Identify and state the function of machine A and B.' and the top of an answer table with rows 'A:', 'Function:' and 'B:'.
notes: The full Q1 stimulus. Letters A and B are printed in bold under the tip of each red arrow and are intact. Machine identification is the answer the question asks for — the crop itself only shows brand decals ('SULKY' on A), so labelMeanings is deliberately empty. The bottom of the crop clips the blank answer table (page furniture), not the figure. SEC acknowledgement for page 3 credits State Examinations Commission and grasstech.ie.

description: Breed-identification plate. At the top the instruction 'Identify any three of the following breeds using the list below' above a pale green option strip with four cells: 'Jersey', 'Blackface mountain', 'Landrace', 'Simmental'. Below it a two-by-two grid of colour photographs. Top left, labelled A: a heavy beef bull standing in a paddock, deep red-brown body with a white head and face, a white band over the shoulders and white lower legs. Top right, labelled B: a large white-pink pig with a long deep body and long ears drooping forward over its face, grazing head-down on grass in front of blue and red hurdles. Bottom left (label cut off): a heavily woolled white sheep in a green field with a black-and-white mottled face, curved horns and coloured ear tags; a small black-and-white lamb's head is visible at the lower edge. Bottom right (label cut off): a fawn/light-tan cow with a darker face, dished forehead, dark muzzle and dark switch on the tail, standing against dark foliage.
notes: UNSAFE TO BIND AS IS. The crop stops at the bottom of the two lower photographs, so the letters C and D — which the paper prints beneath them — are missing entirely, and both lower animals are sliced through the legs. A card asking students to identify A, B, C and D cannot use this crop; it needs a re-extraction that includes the C and D captions. The four option words are printed on the figure but the paper does not pair them with letters, so no labelMeanings are recorded.

description: Q2(b) sheep-breed plate. Stem text at top: 'Jessica is a young sheep farmer and she is looking to buy a ram to breed replacements with her Suffolk cross ewes. Look at the pictures below and answer the questions which follow.' Two colour photographs side by side, each with a bold capital letter centred above it. E (left): a ram standing side-on in a grass field with a hill and a fence post behind, tan/fawn face, ears and lower legs, a slightly paler creamy-tan fleece over a deep body, head turned to the right. F (right): a ram standing side-on in lush deep grass, very blocky heavy white fleece, broad white face with dark grey shading around the eyes and over the muzzle, short ears held horizontally, white legs. Below the photographs: '(i) Identify breed E and F.' with an answer table ruled 'E:' and 'F:', then '(ii) Jessica could choose either breed E or F to cross with her Suffolk cross ewes for replacements in her flock. Advise Jessica with reasons which breed to choose.' and the top of a grey 'Breed:' answer bar.
notes: Both photographs and both letters are complete and legible. Only the grey 'Breed:' answer bar at the very bottom is clipped — page furniture, not figure content. Breed names are the answer being asked for, so none are asserted here. SEC acknowledgement for page 5 credits farmweek.com and pedigreesheep.com.

description: Q5(b) data table with an accompanying photograph. Stem: 'A concentrate ration fed to beef animals has the following composition:'. description: Q6 stimulus. Stem text: 'The safety symbols below are present on a selective herbicide used to control all species of docks in an established grassland sward' (the words 'selective herbicide' underlined). Below: '(a) Explain the underlined term.' with three blank ruled rows, then '(b) Identify the safety symbols labelled A and B above.' and the start of an 'A:' answer box.
notes: Both pictograms and both letters are intact and clearly legible. Near-duplicate of agricultural-science-2022-OL-paper-p09-i1.png — this version is the better one to bind because it also carries the (b) instruction line that names the letters. Only the 'A:' answer box is clipped at the bottom. SEC acknowledgement for page 9 credits hse-network.com, safeopedia.com and State Examinations Commission.

description: Q7(b) photosynthesis diagram — a simple cartoon illustration with a blue sky upper half and a brown soil lower half. In the centre a young green plant with a slender stem, several broad green leaves and a fine root system reaching down into the soil. Top left a yellow sun with radiating rays; a thick black arrow runs from the sun down to the plant's leaves (unlettered — represents light). A second thick black arrow comes in from the left into a lower leaf and is labelled 'Gas A' in bold black text. A pale salmon-pink arrow points out to the right from the upper leaves and is labelled 'Gas B'. A second pale salmon-pink arrow points down and to the right away from the plant and is labelled only with the bold letter 'C'. At the bottom left a bold white 'Water' label with a cluster of small blue droplets sits beside a black arrow running rightwards through the soil into the plant's roots. Printed beside the diagram: 'Photosynthesis is the method by which green plants make their own food using chlorophyll. (i) Identify what A, B and C are representing in the picture illustrating photosynthesis.' with an answer table ruled 'A:', 'B:', 'C:', then '(ii) Describe two ways a leaf is adapted to carry out photosynthesis.'

Below: '(a) Identify each piece of equipment A and B above.' with an answer table ruled 'A:' and 'B:', then '(b) State a suitable prediction for this investigation.'
notes: Both items and both letters are complete. Naming the equipment is the answer the question wants, so no labelMeanings are asserted; the descriptions above are of visible form only. description: Q17(a) stimulus panel. Already, automated or robotic milking machines are in use in Ireland and over 50% of all new milking machines installed in the European Union (EU) are automated. Robotic milking has a number of advantages. There is more consistency, reduced labour costs, the possibility of increased milking frequency (three times a day) and better overall herd management.' with the source line '(Adapted from Science and Technology in Action, 2013)' beneath the box. Inset at the top right of the panel is a colour photograph of a robotic milking unit inside a shed: a red-panelled machine with 'ASTRONAUT' printed across the top, galvanised rails forming the entry race, and a black-and-white cow standing in the unit. The examinable content is the article prose, which is also available from the paper's text layer. The photo is a branded robotic milking unit (the word ASTRONAUT is legible on it) and is not labelled or lettered.

description: A coloured line-art laboratory bench scene for a soil pH investigation, drawn on a brown wooden bench that runs the full width. Working left to right the apparatus shown is: (1) a small beaker of pale liquid holding an upright yellow/orange test strip whose submerged tip has turned green — a blue arrow labelled A points to this strip; (2) a handheld grey electronic meter with a digital display reading '6.5' above the word 'pH' and two round green buttons, its cable running down into a second beaker of liquid — a black arrow labelled in words 'pH probe' points to this meter; (3) a beaker of pale green liquid with a dropper/pipette dipped into it — a black arrow labelled in words 'Universal Indicator' points to the dropper tip; (4) a tall graduated measuring cylinder with graduation marks, part filled with pale blue liquid, with a conical filter funnel and folded filter paper seated in its mouth holding a dark brown mass of soil, filtrate draining into the cylinder — a blue arrow labelled B points to the top of this cylinder/funnel assembly; (5) a small beaker holding brown soil with a long spatula/stirring rod in it, with a conical flask tipped over it pouring water in; (6) an electronic top-pan balance with a blue digital display reading '100.00 g', carrying a weighing boat with a lump of brown soil on it — a blue arrow labelled C points to the balance pan. Above the drawing is the printed question text: 'Answer any ten questions. Each question carries 10 marks. Question 1. An agricultural science student wanted to test the pH of a sample of soil before deciding what crops to sow.' Below the drawing is part (a) 'Identify any two pieces of equipment labelled A, B or C required for this investigation.' and a three-row blank answer table with the row stubs A:, B:, C:.
notes: The three lettered blue arrows are the examinable labels for Q1(a); the two black word-labels ('pH probe', 'Universal Indicator') are given by the paper and are NOT part of the lettered answer. The digital pH meter reading 6.5 is the value needed for Q1(b) 'State the pH of the soil filtrate'. Whole drawing sits inside the crop with all three letters intact; only the following line of question prose ('(b) State the pH of the soil filtrate') is sliced by the bottom edge, so the figure itself is safe. labelMeanings left empty because the figure does not tie any word to A, B or C.

description: A three-panel table of hand-drawn line diagrams showing the development of a ruminant stomach. The table has a grey header row with three red bold column headings: 'First week', '3 to 4 months', 'Maturity'. Each cell below contains an outline drawing of the four-chambered stomach in side view, with a short tube (the oesophagus) entering at the left. In every panel three parts are named in words with black leader arrows — 'Rumen' (arrow into the large rounded sac), 'Omasum' (arrow into the small hatched/dotted chamber at the upper right) and 'Reticulum' (arrow up into the chamber at the lower right) — and a fourth part is marked only by a dark blue upward arrow with a red capital letter A beneath it, pointing into the elongated lower chamber that runs along the bottom of the drawing. The proportions change across the panels: in 'First week' the chamber marked A is large relative to a small rumen; by '3 to 4 months' the rumen has grown; at 'Maturity' the rumen is by far the largest chamber and the chamber marked A is a long narrow sac beneath it. Above the table a line of question prose is sliced by the crop edge ('...Analyse the diagrams and answer the questions which follow' is legible below it). Beneath the table is '(i) Identify the stomach chamber A.' with a blank answer box, and '(ii) Explain the changes in the structure of the ruminant stomach as the animal gets older.'
notes: A is the only letter and is deliberately the unknown the student must name in (i); the figure itself gives no word for it, so labelMeanings is empty — the other three chambers are already named in words in every panel (rumen, omasum, reticulum) and those names are recorded in the description, not attributed to A. The same red A appears in all three panels pointing to the same chamber. Table and all three panels including the right-hand border are fully inside the crop (verified by zooming the right edge); only the top line of question prose is sliced. Near-duplicate of p12-i1, which is a slightly tighter crop of the same table.

description: The same three-panel ruminant stomach development table, cropped tighter. A grey header row carries three red bold headings: 'First week', '3 to 4 months', 'Maturity'. description: A schematic diagram of gene editing with CRISPR-Cas9, drawn as horizontal capsule-shaped bars representing lengths of DNA. Two diagonal arrows then lead down to two different outcomes. Left outcome: a single rejoined bar, red - blue - red, i.e. the cut has simply been sealed. Right outcome: a longer bar reading red - blue - green - blue - red, where a pale green segment has been placed between the two blue pieces; the word 'Insertion' labels this green segment, and a curved arrow rises to it from a separate small pale green bar drawn on its own at the bottom right of the diagram. Above the diagram the printed stem is partly sliced by the crop edge but reads '...developing new plant varieties. The diagram shows a gene being edited using the tool CRISPR-Cas9.' Below is '(i) With the aid of the diagram above, explain how the gene editing process works.' with the start of a blank ruled answer box.

notes: Overlaps p03-i0, which holds the complete A and B panels. Photo C is complete and legible here but photo B is sliced through, so this crop must not be bound as the A/B/C figure. The yellow arrow marks the hurdle joining clamp, i.e. the item to be identified in C.

description: Question 2(a)(i) breed-identification figure: 'Identify any two of the following breeds.' Three colour photographs in a row, each headed by a bold letter, with an empty answer box beneath each. A: a pale pink-and-white pig standing in full profile on grass in front of a show pen rail, long-bodied with a straight back, large forward-drooping lop ears covering the eye, curly tail visible at the rear. B: a close-up of a sheep's head and neck angled over a wooden pen rail - the head carries no wool, the skin is dark blue-grey showing through fine white hair, the nose is strongly arched (Roman), the muzzle black, the ears long and erect with a yellow tag in the near ear, and a dense curly cream-brown fleece begins at the shoulder. C: a heavily muscled bull standing in a grass field, broken tan/golden-brown and white coat with large white patches on the flank, white underline, white lower legs and a white head with a curly forehead; a second dark red animal is just visible at the right. Under the photos the answer row is blank. Above, the sliced remains of the line 'Question 2   Answer either (a) or (b).' Below the photos, '(ii) The sheep in B in part (i) above is known for its prolificacy. Explain the underlined term.'
notes: The right edge slices photo C and its answer box (26% ink on the last pixel column), and the top edge cuts through the 'Question 2 / Answer either (a) or (b)' line - so this crop is not safe to bind despite all three animals being recognisable. p04-i1 is the same crop offset by 2 pixels and has the identical defect. Breeds deliberately not named here; visually A reads as a lop-eared white pig, B as a blue-faced Roman-nosed sheep and C as a tan-and-white continental beef bull, but the naming is the scheme's job.

description: Pixel-for-pixel the same Question 2(a)(i) breed figure as p04-i0, shifted up by two pixels: three lettered colour photographs in a row - A a pale pink-and-white long-bodied pig with large drooping lop ears standing in profile on grass by a show rail; B a close-up of a woolless blue-grey sheep head with white hair, strongly arched Roman nose, black muzzle, long erect ears, yellow ear tag and a dense curly cream fleece at the shoulder, resting over a wooden pen rail; C a heavily muscled tan-and-white bull with a white head, white flank patches and white lower legs standing in grass. description: The lower two-thirds of the Irish Moiled article box used as the stimulus for Question 2(b). Body prose reads: 'They are generally easy to handle with a placid docile temperament. Surplus males sell well as steers finishing between 20-24 months on good quality forage diet to carcass weights from 220-260kg. The beef is of superb quality with a distinctive flavour. The cow can be relied upon to produce a calf every 12 months if kept in good health and body condition. They will calve to a continental bull without difficulty and will continue to breed satisfactorily until at least ten years of age. Tradition has it that they are big bellied to consume and digest large quantities of poorer quality forage which was their traditional diet. They can be termed ready browsers because they will graze willow, ash and ivy, which makes them ideal in extensive or conservation grazing situations. They are sound in hoof and leg and at home on most types of terrain. They grow a thick winter coat and out-winter happily although being a heavy animal they will poach soft ground.' Attribution '(Adapted from thecattlesite.com)' sits under the box, followed by '(i) Explain the underlined term.' and a blank answer box. Set into the prose on the right is a colour photograph of a small group of red-roan and white cattle standing in a grass field - a white-and-red cow in the foreground with a smaller white calf beside her and two more red-and-white animals behind. Along the very top edge, a sliced band of a second photograph shows only the white legs and lower bodies of cattle on grass.
notes: Article stimulus, not a referenced figure - the question asks students to read the text, and the cattle photographs are illustrative. Overlaps p05-i1, which holds the top of the same article. Top edge slices a photograph; the article's left border is flush with the crop edge (80% ink on the first column).

It is a hornless medium sized breed with a mature cow weighing up to 650kg. Traditionally a dairy cow with yields of up to 5000 litres, it has earned the reputation as a truly dual purpose breed. In the suckler herd the cow will go into a negative energy balance (underlined) to ensure the calf gets the best start in life.' The prose continues across the full width: 'They are generally easy to handle with a placid docile temperament. Surplus males sell well as steers finishing between 20-24 months on good quality forage diet to carcass weights from 220-260kg. The beef is of superb quality with a distinctive flavour. The cow can be relied upon to produce a calf every 12 months if kept in good health and body condition. They will calve to a continental bull without difficulty and will continue to breed satisfactorily until at least ten years of age. Tradition has it that they are big bellied to consume and...' where the text is cut. A second photograph, of a group of red-and-white and white cattle with a calf in a field, is set into the lower right and is sliced by the bottom edge.
notes: Article stimulus rather than an examined figure. Overlaps p05-i0 (which carries the tail of the same article). Bottom edge cuts both the prose and the second photograph; the article box border is flush with the left crop edge.

description: The Question 3(a) grassland-management diagram, drawn as a cross-section through a sward with the soil shown as a graded brown-to-tan block below a black ground line. Three grass plants stand side by side, decreasing in size from left to right: the left plant has tall abundant blue-green leaves and a deep, dense, heavily branched black root system reaching most of the way down the soil block; the middle plant is shorter with fewer leaves and a noticeably shallower, less branched root mass; the right plant is a small sparse tuft with only a short shallow bunch of roots. A red bracket on the left labels the left-hand sward height 'Post grazing stubble 4cm'; an orange bracket on the right labels the short right-hand sward 'Post grazing stubble 2cm'; a blue bracket down the left side of the soil block labels the whole below-ground area 'Root responses'. Beneath the drawing a table begins, its first row reading 'Grazing period | Short (1 - 2 days) | Long (6 - 7 days) | Continuous (2 - 3 months)', each column heading sitting under the corresponding plant. Above the drawing, the sliced line 'Analyse the diagram and answer the questions that follow.'
notes: The second table row, 'Recovery allowed | Long | Short | None', is cut off below the bottom edge, and the instruction line is sliced at the top - so the figure is incomplete even though the drawing itself is intact. This is the better of the two p06 crops (p06-i1 has no table at all). The figure uses word labels only, no letter labels: 'Post grazing stubble 4cm', 'Post grazing stubble 2cm', 'Root responses', plus the grazing-period column headings.

description: A tighter crop of the same Question 3(a) grassland cross-section: three grass plants of decreasing size standing on a black ground line above a graded brown-to-tan soil block, with root systems that shrink from a deep, dense, heavily branched mass under the tallest plant, to a shallower branched mass under the middle plant, to a short sparse bunch under the smallest plant on the right. A red bracket on the left carries 'Post grazing stubble 4cm', an orange bracket on the right carries 'Post grazing stubble 2cm', and a blue bracket down the left of the soil carries 'Root responses'. The tips of the tallest grass leaves and the top of the red bracket run off the top edge, and the crop stops at the ground/soil block with no table beneath.
notes: Duplicates the drawing in p06-i0 but is worse: the top edge slices the tallest leaves and the top of the red 4cm bracket, and the whole grazing-period/recovery table that the question depends on is absent. Prefer p06-i0 if either is ever used, and even that one is missing the 'Recovery allowed' row.

description: Question 3(b) in full: the centred word 'Or', then '(b) Rotational (paddock) grazing is described as a sustainable farming practice. description: The Question 5(a) cereal-identification figure, a two-row grid with three lettered columns A, B and C. Row 1 (marked by a red '1' on the left) holds three close-up colour photographs of the leaf/stem junction of a young cereal plant. The A photograph shows a green stem where the leaf blade meets the sheath with no obvious clasping appendages. The B photograph shows a pale green collar at the leaf base with a white arrow pointing to it from a white callout box lettered 'Auricles'. The C photograph shows a leaf sheath wrapping the stem with a second white arrow, from the same 'Auricles' callout, pointing to a pale clasping structure at the collar. Bold dark blue captions run beneath row 1, one under each column: under A 'No auricles and leaf margins are hairless', under B 'Well-developed hairy auricles', under C 'Large, hairless auricles'. Row 2 (marked by a red '2') holds three ripening-crop photographs: under A a field of pale golden cereal whose seeds hang on fine spreading branches in an open, drooping panicle; under B a field of upright golden ears packed in a compact spike with short bristles; under C a close-up of a green ear with long straight awns radiating out from the top. Instruction text above reads 'Each crop at its ripening stage is shown for reference in row 2. Assist farmers by identifying A, B and C as barley, wheat or oats.'

labelMeanings.meaning: printed caption under column A: 'No auricles and leaf margins are hairless'
printed caption under column B: 'Well-developed hairy auricles'
printed caption under column C: 'Large, hairless auricles'
row 1 - the stage each crop was at when the farm was visited (close-ups of the leaf collar / auricle region)
row 2 - the same crop shown at its ripening stage, given for reference

notes: High-value photo-identification figure, but the bottom edge cuts straight through the three row-2 ripening photographs (87% ink on the last pixel row), so it must be re-cropped before binding. The word 'Auricles' is a single callout box whose two arrows point into the B and C photographs only; there is no arrow into A. The A/B/C captions listed in labelMeanings are printed on the figure itself, not inferred - but they are auricle descriptions, not crop names, so the barley/wheat/oats answer still belongs to the marking scheme.
